text: In a meritocracy-oriented cultural context, visible merit serves as the key yardstick for distinguishing winners from losers ( Wu and Gao, 2023 ). Juvenile offenders, marked by low socioeconomic status, limited educational attainment, and a conspicuous deviant label, are readily categorized as “incompetent” or “morally tainted” failures, incurring multiple layers of identity threat. A strong societal meritocratic climate further consolidates the intergroup boundary between them and mainstream groups, weakening their willingness to integrate. The social disconnection arising from impaired collective self-esteem is often accompanied by heightened negative affect, reduced self-regulation, and social withdrawal, rendering them more susceptible to internalizing external devaluation as self-stigma ( Baumeister et al., 2007 ). Moreover, the deindividuation effect of a stigmatized identity can prompt these adolescents to adopt attitudes and behaviors consistent with the deviant stereotype, reinforcing delinquent patterns and impeding positive identity reconstruction ( Jetten et al., 2015 ).
source_label: Perceived societal meritocratic climate and self-stigma among adolescents in conflict with the law: the mediating role of collective self-esteem and social disconnection
